answers.children: Akitas can be moderately good with children when raised together but their large powerful build and protective instincts require close supervision with smaller kids. Their independent nature and tolerance for rough play are limited by the guarding background that made them track and hold large game in Japan's rugged mountains so they may interpret sudden movements as threats. (PawLabs child-friendly score: 6/10)
answers.other-pets: Akitas do not get along reliably with other pets especially dogs of the same sex because their protective temperament leads to aloofness or aggression toward strangers and other animals. Bred to hunt bear boar and deer in pairs they show strong territorial instincts that make introducing new pets challenging and require careful management to avoid tense standoffs.
answers.exercise: Akitas need one hour of daily exercise such as brisk walks or play in a secure yard to maintain their muscular heavy frame. Without it their independent spirit can lead to boredom-driven stubbornness and destructive behaviour while their build suited to harsh winters tires faster in heat so they prefer cooler conditions and mental challenges like dragging heavy objects over marathon running.
answers.shedding: Yes — Akitas shed heavily especially during seasonal blows because their medium double coat is thick and dense to protect against northern Japan's harsh winters. The undercoat releases in large quantities while the outer layer traps loose hair around the home and the powerful build means more volume of fur to clear after each blow.
answers.hypoallergenic: Akitas have a medium double coat that sheds noticeably and releases dander into the home. Their thick undercoat traps hair and requires regular grooming to manage loose fur around the house. No breed is genuinely hypoallergenic and Akitas are not among those usually suggested to allergy sufferers.
answers.training: Akitas are not easy to train because their stubborn independent nature and loyalty focused on family rather than seeking approval make them challenging for novices. Originally bred to hunt large game with minimal direction in Japan's mountains their intelligence of seven out of ten is paired with a protective streak that leads them to decide when commands matter resulting in selective obedience.
answers.lifespan: Akitas live 10-14 years and their powerful muscular build developed for hunting in rugged terrain contributes to a health robustness score of six out of ten. The thick double coat that protected them from northern Japan's harsh winters supports a sturdy frame but their large size from 70 to 130 pounds places demands on joints and heart so consistent exercise helps maintain condition throughout their adult years.
answers.size: Adult Akitas weigh 70-130 lb and stand 24-28 in tall at the shoulder with a bear-like imposing build that feels substantial in the home. Their strong muscular frame bred for holding large game such as bear and boar in Japan's mountains means they take up significant space when lying near their owner and their protective presence can dominate a room while the heavy substance of the body requires sturdy furniture and careful navigation indoors.
answers.barking: Akitas do not bark a lot and tend to stay quiet unless issuing a low warning rumble at perceived threats. Their protective and loyal temperament combined with a history as guardians for samurai means they rely more on their strong imposing presence and stoic watchfulness than frequent vocalisation making them reserved watchdogs that alert through body language rather than noise.
answers.apartment: Akitas can live in an apartment if given sufficient daily exercise and mental stimulation because their calm independent temperament allows them to settle indoors quietly. The low barking level of three out of ten and moderate energy suit a settled lifestyle but their large powerful build and protective instincts require secure space to move and prevent frustration from lack of activity.
answers.first-time: Akitas are not a good first dog because their stubbornness and independent nature demand an experienced handler who can manage the protective instincts. Deep loyalty to family is paired with aloofness toward strangers and other dogs so the guarding background that made them prized by samurai requires firm consistent leadership that novices may find overwhelming.
